govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIWarrenCommis:
An FBI report numbered ZBC-1 records an interview on December 11, 1963 at St. David's Hospital in Austin. The patient was Governor John Connally of Texas, wounded in the Dallas shooting that killed President Kennedy. From his hospital bed, Connally recounted his experience of the shots.

Connally was the closest surviving witness to the president at the moment of the shooting. What he remembered about the shots, their order, and his own wounds became key evidence. The report fixes that memory nineteen days after the event, in the words the Bureau wrote down.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KinneyEdwardChr:
Harold Weisberg spent decades challenging the official account of the Kennedy assassination, and this April 25 letter shows his method. His subject is the Navy's refusal to say who its Surgeon General was. The letter also takes up the Sibert-O'Neill report and the testimony of Dr. Pierre Finck, who was involved in the autopsy.

FBI agents James Sibert and Francis O'Neill filed their report on the autopsy of President Kennedy. Finck's testimony about that examination became a point of dispute among researchers. Weisberg argues that official silence on such small, checkable points hides basic facts. The letter presses an agency on details and builds a case from its answers.
hartmann-iwein-benecke-lachmann:
Hartmann von Aue retold the tale of Yvain in German as Iwein, and the Benecke and Lachmann edition keeps that text in print. The version here, revised by Wolff, runs the full 8,165 verses. Iwein is a knight of Arthur's court who wins a wife and a land.

Iwein breaks his word to his lady and loses her love and his wits at once. Mad in the woods, he is healed and must climb back by deeds of service. A lion he saves fights at his side the rest of the way. The poem stands as a peak of medieval German courtly romance.
grillparzer-der-arme-spielmann:
A poor street fiddler in Vienna plays badly, loves hopelessly, and carries a whole life of sorrow in his music. Grillparzer's Der arme Spielmann, given here in German, is his most famous story. A festival-goer narrates, slowly coming to understand the mocked old musician he first pitied from a distance.

The fiddler's tale unfolds in layers: a lost inheritance, a patient love, a flood, and music as the vessel of it all. Unrecognized genius and quiet sanctity meet in one humble figure. Critics rank the novella among the great short works of world literature. Its portrait of failure transfigured by devotion has moved readers for generations. Few Austrian stories are loved more tenderly.
hofmannsthal-jedermann:
A rich man named Everyman receives a summons from Death and finds his companions unwilling to follow. Hugo von Hofmannsthal's Jedermann, from 1911 and given here in German, retells the medieval morality play for modern audiences. Performed every summer at the Salzburg Festival since 1920, it has become Austria's most beloved play.

Medieval in form and modern in feeling, the drama asks what a life is worth when the accounts are finally called. Money, friends, and good deeds each answer the summons in turn. Hofmannsthal's verse gives the old allegory fresh music and ache. Open-air performances before Salzburg cathedral made the play a national ritual. The German text lets readers hear why it holds the stage so firmly.
